# Jlisten2me Journal, full text

> Jlisten2me is a confidential one-hour listening service in Austin, Texas, by phone or in person. Not therapy, not coaching. Nothing recorded, no notes kept.

Every published journal article, newest first. None is drawn from a session.

---

## When your grown child stopped speaking to you

URL: https://jlisten2me.com/journal/grown-child-stopped-speaking/
Published: 2026-11-24
Author: John Parsons

The last message is still on your phone.
You've read it more times than you'd admit, looking for the sentence that explains everything.
When someone at work or in the checkout line asks how the kids are, you have a short answer ready that ends the conversation.
The holidays are coming, and there's a place at the table you've stopped setting.

Nobody holds a service for this. Nobody brings food. Nobody marks a date on the calendar. There was a last call, or a last visit, or a message that said more than you were ready for. Then quiet.

Some days you're sure it's all your fault and you go over every year of their childhood looking for the moment. Other days you can't make sense of it at all. Some nights you start a letter in your head. You apologize, then explain, then take the explanation back, then start over. You haven't sent it. You aren't sure you will. If there are grandchildren, you think about them on birthdays, and you count how old they are now.

## Who can't hear this

Your friends are the first people you'd normally turn to, and this is the hardest thing to tell them. There's a shame attached to it that a divorce or a layoff doesn't carry. Saying "my child won't speak to me" feels like handing people a verdict on your parenting. And the friends who do know tend to push. Just reach out. Life's too short. Show up at the door. They want it fixed, and they mean it kindly, and each suggestion lands as one more thing you've apparently failed to try.

Your other children, if you have them, are caught in the middle already. Some of them may still be in touch with their brother or sister. Anything you say to them becomes a message, or a burden, or a reason to pick a side. You don't want to put them there, so you talk to them about everything else.

Your spouse or partner is in it with you, and that makes it harder to talk to them about it. They grieve on a different schedule. They might be angry when you're sad, or quiet when you need to talk. Sometimes they blame you, or themselves, or the child, and every conversation drifts toward who did what. You can't think out loud with someone who's carrying their own half of it.

## What it sounds like out loud

I don't know what happened between you and your child, and I won't guess. That's yours to tell, in whatever order it comes out, from whatever side you're standing on that day.

Saying a thing like this to another person changes how it sits. You hear yourself say "I miss them" and "I'm angry with them" inside a minute and both stay true. You hear which memories you go to first. You might read the letter out loud, the one you haven't sent, and notice which lines you rush through and which ones you slow down on.

You can say the things you'd never say to your friends, like how much you dread the holidays, or how you skip past certain photos on your phone. You can say you're afraid you deserve it. You can say you're sure you don't. Nobody in the room hands you a ruling either way.

## The hour

You can call from anywhere for $60, or meet in person in Austin for $200, by request, at a public spot we agree on, on one of a few Wednesdays a month at noon. You can book under a first name. Stripe takes the payment, so I never see your card.

At the start you tell me whether you want to be talked up or want to let it out. I won't tell you whether to reach out, and I won't take sides. If you ask for my thoughts out loud, I'll give them, and otherwise I'll just listen. If you need to sit quiet for a while, that's fine.

I don't take notes and nothing is recorded. I don't know your family and I won't meet them. What you say about your child, and about yourself, goes nowhere after the hour.

## What an hour can't do

An hour of listening won't bring your child back or tell you what went wrong. If you want to understand what happened, prepare for a conversation that may or may not come, or work through it over time, a family therapist is the right person. Support groups for estranged parents put you with people who know exactly what a quiet holiday sounds like, and some of them have been at it for years.

If you're in crisis, call or text 988 in the US.

If you'd like to say it to someone who has no verdict on it, a phone hour is $60 and you can book it under a first name. Pick an hour.

## When you have to give the eulogy and it's complicated

URL: https://jlisten2me.com/journal/complicated-eulogy/
Published: 2026-11-17
Author: John Parsons

Someone in the family asked you to speak, and you said yes before you'd thought it through.
Now there's a blank page, a service in a few days, and a parent you had a hard time loving some years.
Everyone will be looking at you while you talk about them.
You want to tell the truth, and you don't want to hurt anyone, and you aren't sure those fit in the same five minutes.

You keep hearing the old rule in your head: if you can't say something nice, don't say anything at all. You can say nice things. There were good days, and you remember them. There were also years you'd rather not describe, and pretending they didn't happen feels like a lie told from a podium.

So you write a paragraph and delete it. You list their achievements and it reads like a résumé of a stranger. Then you remember the way they hummed while they cooked, or the car they kept far too long, and you start to see a version you could stand behind. Small, ordinary details often hold more truth than a list of accomplishments, and they let you be honest without settling scores.

## Why it's hard to talk this through with family

The people you'd normally run this past are grieving the same person, and they may have known a different one.

Your siblings might want a clean, warm version. Maybe they had an easier relationship with your parent, or maybe they've decided that today is no time for anything else. Either way, if you start explaining what you're struggling with, it can turn into an argument about whose memories count.

Your surviving parent, aunts, uncles, and family friends will be in the front rows. They want to hear something comforting, and some of them would be shocked by the version you carry. You can't test your doubts on them without making the week harder for everybody.

Your spouse or partner has probably heard the whole story already, more than once. They'll listen again, because they love you, and you can see it wearing on them. They may also have strong feelings about your parent that pull the conversation somewhere else.

Friends who never met your parent can be supportive, and they don't have much to hold onto. They'll tell you whatever you write will be fine.

That leaves you writing and rewriting alone, late at night, with no one to read it to.

## Saying the unsaid version first

There's usually a version of this eulogy you'd never give. The one with the anger in it, the disappointments, the thing they said that you've carried for years. It sits underneath every draft and makes them all feel false.

Saying that version out loud, somewhere safe, can take some of the pressure off it. Once another person has heard it, it may push less hard on the version you'll actually read. The true, kind sentences can come more easily after that, once you've stopped fighting to keep the other ones in.

Then there's the delivery itself. Reading it aloud is different from reading it in your head. You'll find the line that catches in your throat. Many people practice it out loud enough times the night before that they've cried it out already, and then bring a printed copy and a glass of water to the podium. Hearing yourself get through it once, start to finish, makes the morning less of an unknown.

## How the hour works

You can book a phone hour from anywhere, or meet in person in Austin on a few Wednesdays a month at noon, at a public spot we agree on after you book. Use a first name if you like. Stripe takes the payment and I never see your card.

At the start you say whether you want to be talked up or want to let it out. You might spend the first half telling me who your parent really was, all of it, and the second half reading me the eulogy. If tomorrow is the big day, run it at me first. Read it as many times as you need. If you want my honest reaction to a line, ask out loud and I'll give it. Otherwise I just listen, and silence is fine.

Nothing is recorded. I don't keep notes, and nothing you tell me gets repeated or used as an example. I never knew your parent, and I'm not sitting in the pews.

## What I can't do for you

An hour of listening won't settle how you feel about your parent, and it won't write the eulogy for you. Grief after a hard relationship can be tangled for a long time, with relief, guilt, and sadness arriving together. A grief counselor works with exactly that, and is worth seeing if it keeps returning after the service is over. A licensed therapist is also a good choice if old family hurts have come back up with it.

If you're in crisis, call or text 988 in the US.

If you need to say all of it before you stand up and say the right part, a phone hour is $60 and you can book it under a first name. Reserve an hour.

## When you're looking for a new job and haven't told anyone at home

URL: https://jlisten2me.com/journal/secret-job-search/
Published: 2026-11-10
Author: John Parsons

You told your manager it was a dentist appointment.
The interview was at eight, so you could be at your desk by ten looking like you'd hit traffic.
You took the recruiter's call in the car in a parking garage, engine running for the air conditioning.
At dinner, when your partner asked about your day, you said it was fine.

A quiet job search runs on small covers. Each one is harmless by itself. Added together, they make two lives, and you're keeping both going while doing your current job well enough that nobody looks twice.

## Why it's staying quiet for now

Your boss is the obvious one. Tell them you're looking and you've more or less given notice, without an offer to land on. You might get passed over for the next project, or eased toward the door before you're ready to walk through it. So you watch for small signs instead. You wonder whether they saw that you updated your profile. You wonder whether the last-minute "can you stay late Thursday" is a test.

Coworkers notice more than you'd like. The second doctor's appointment in a month, the nicer shirt on a Tuesday, the long lunch that ends with you coming back a little flushed. Even a work friend you trust can let something slip in a meeting without meaning to. Once one person knows, you're managing what they know too.

Your partner is the harder one, and the reasons are usually kind ones. Maybe you don't want to raise their hopes. If you mention the better salary or the shorter commute and then don't get it, they'll be disappointed along with you, and you'd rather carry that alone. Or maybe you can already hear the argument: the benefits, the stability, the timing, whether this is the right year to take a risk. You'd rather have that conversation with an offer in hand, when there's something real to talk about.

So the plan is to tell them once it's settled. Meanwhile, everything that happens in between goes nowhere. The interview that went great and the one where you blanked on an easy question. The final round that ended with a warm handshake and then a silence that keeps going. You come home from each of those and have to act like it was a normal day.

Friends would listen, but a lot of them know your partner, and the next time everyone's at the same table someone might ask how the search is going. Keeping a secret from your partner is hard enough without spreading it around.

## Letting the cover story drop for an hour

Holding all of this alone makes it louder than it needs to be. Each rejection rattles around with nowhere to land. Each good sign builds into a fantasy you can't check against anyone.

Saying it to another person puts it back in proportion. You hear yourself describe the job you're chasing, and you can tell from your own voice whether you want it or just want out. You hear how you talk about the job you have, which might be harsher than you realized, or softer. Sometimes you notice that the hardest part of the whole thing is the hiding, and that the search itself is going better than it felt.

It also helps to have one place where the cover story can come off. For an hour you don't have to remember which excuse you used with whom.

## How a call fits around a workday

You can call from anywhere, which works well from a parked car on a lunch break. If you're in Austin, we can meet in person on one of a few Wednesdays a month at noon, at a public spot we settle on after you book. A first name is enough. Stripe handles the payment, so I never see your card.

When we start, you tell me whether you want to be talked up before the next interview or want to let it out about the last one. I won't give advice unless you ask for it out loud. Silence is fine if you need a second to think.

I don't take notes and nothing is recorded. I don't know your boss, your coworkers, or your partner, and nothing you tell me gets repeated or used as an example. When the call ends, the secret is still yours to tell when you're ready.

## What a career coach is for

An hour of being heard won't get you the job, and I won't rewrite your resume or coach you through salary talks. If you want help with the search itself, a career coach is the right person for that. If the strain of keeping it quiet has started following you into your sleep or your relationship, a licensed therapist can help you sort through it.

If you're in crisis, call or text 988 in the US.

If you need somewhere to put all this between interviews, a phone hour is $60, booked under a first name. Choose a time.

## When you promised your mom you'd never put her in a home

URL: https://jlisten2me.com/journal/promised-never-a-home/
Published: 2026-11-03
Author: John Parsons

You said it years ago, probably at a kitchen table, and you meant every word.
Never. You'd never put her in one of those places.
Then came the falls, the burner left on, the nights she didn't know which house she was in.
Now she lives in a room with her name on the door, and you drive home from visits feeling two things at once.
One of them is relief, and that's the one you can't say.

The tours blurred together after a while. The lobby with the fish tank, the activity calendar by the elevator, the nurse who smiled at your mother and talked to you over her head. You signed the papers. You've heard her ask, sometimes more than once in a visit, when she can go home. Meanwhile the family house went on the market, and you spent a weekend sorting her recipe cards into boxes marked keep and donate.

Then a few weeks passed. You slept through the night. You went to the grocery store without checking your phone in every aisle. And each time you notice how much lighter you feel, the promise comes back around and sits on your chest.

## The people you'd normally tell

Your mom is the one you'd have told everything to, once. You can't tell her this. When she asks to go home, you say soon, or you talk about the weather, and you walk out to the parking lot carrying the answer you didn't give.

Your brothers and sisters have opinions, and the ones who live farthest away tend to have the most. They call to ask whether you really looked at enough places, whether she's eating, whether that aide seemed rough with her. If you told them you were relieved, you'd be handing them proof of something they already half believe about you. So you report the facts and keep the rest.

Your spouse or partner lived through the hard years beside you. They drove her to appointments, gave up weekends, and heard about all of it every night for longer than either of you wants to count. They're glad it's settled, and they're tired of the subject. You can see it on their face when you bring it up again, so you've mostly stopped bringing it up.

Friends mean well. Most of them haven't done this yet. They tell you that you did the right thing, which is kind, and it closes the conversation right where you needed it to open. A few tell you they could never do that to their own mother, and you add it to the pile.

## When relief and guilt share a sentence

Relief and guilt arrive in your head together and argue, and the argument never finishes because nobody hears the whole thing.

Saying it to another person puts it in some kind of order. You start telling it as a story about her, and somewhere along the way it becomes a story about you, about the years you were the one who got the calls. You describe the last bad night at the house and hear how close it came. You say the promise out loud, the actual words, and you notice who you were when you made it and what you knew back then.

You might get to the word relief halfway through the hour, or at the very end, or in the first minute because it's been waiting by the door. Whenever it comes out, nobody in the room flinches, and you get to keep talking. You can also say that you check on her care more than you need to, that you read the staff's faces at every visit, that part of you is waiting to be caught doing something wrong.

## How the hour goes

You can call from anywhere for $60, or meet me in person in Austin at a public spot we agree on, on one of a few Wednesdays a month at noon. Book under a first name if you like. Stripe takes the payment, so I never see your card.

At the start you tell me whether you want to be talked up or want to let it out. Some days you'll want someone to point out how much you carried. Other days you'll want to say the ugly parts and have them heard. Either is fine. I won't give advice unless you ask for it out loud. If you go quiet for a while, that's fine too.

I don't take notes and nothing is recorded. I've never met your mother or your siblings, and I have no opinion about the place you chose. When we hang up, what you said goes with you and nowhere else.

## Where an hour stops

An hour of listening won't tell you whether her care is good enough, and it won't settle anything about the house, the money, or the paperwork. If you're worried about how she's being looked after, or you're weighing a move to a different place, a geriatric care manager or the facility's social worker knows what to look for and what to ask. If the guilt keeps coming back week after week, a caregiver support group puts you in a room with people who made the same promise and had to set it down. For Medicaid, powers of attorney, and selling the house, you need an elder law attorney.

If you're in crisis, call or text 988 in the US.

If you'd like to say all of it once, to someone outside the family, a phone hour is $60 and you can book it under a first name. Find a time.

## When you're not sure you can make payroll

URL: https://jlisten2me.com/journal/not-sure-you-can-make-payroll/
Published: 2026-10-27
Author: John Parsons

It's two days before payday and you've checked the bank balance four times since breakfast.
You already know what it says.
Last time you covered the gap with your own savings, and the time before that with a credit card.
Out on the floor, your people are working like it's any other week, because as far as they know, it is.

Running a small business with employees means carrying a number nobody else sees. Payday comes on a schedule. Customers pay when they pay. In the space between those two facts you move money around, wait on a check, push a supplier, and do the math again at night when you can't sleep.

What makes it heavy is who's on the other end. Every person on payroll has rent, kids, a car payment, a plan for the weekend. You know some of their families. You hired them, and somewhere along the way you started feeling responsible for more than their hourly rate. So you keep paying them first, and you pay yourself last or not at all, and you tell yourself next month will be better.

Meanwhile other things fray. You're short with the people at home. You skip the doctor's appointment because it's a weekday and you can't leave. Friends stop inviting you to things because you always say you're slammed.

## Why the people around you can't hear it

Your employees are the first people affected, and the last people you can tell. Maybe you've told them part of it, that things are tight, that you're watching costs. You haven't told them you're not sure about the next run. If you did, the ones with the most options would start looking, and they'd be right to. Losing your best people in a tight month makes the next tight month worse.

Your spouse or partner probably knows money is a worry. They may not know that the savings account you both think of as a cushion has been quietly feeding payroll. Telling them means telling them that, and watching the worry move into their face and stay there. Your kids, your parents, your siblings all get a version that sounds fine, because you don't want them carrying it.

Other business owners in town seem like natural people to talk to, and some of them would understand better than anyone. They're also your competitors, or friends with your competitors, or people who know your suppliers and your landlord. In a local business community, "I heard they're struggling" travels quickly, and it changes how people treat you. Some of them would mean well. A few might see an opening.

Your banker and your accountant need the facts, and you'll give them the facts. They don't need to hear how it feels to lie awake doing the math about people you care about. That part has nowhere to go.

## What saying it out loud does

When you carry a number like this alone, it grows. It shows up at dinner, in the shower, at your kid's game. It turns into a running list of what could go wrong, each item worse than the last.

Saying it to another person shrinks it back to its actual size. You have to put it in sentences: what's coming in, what's going out, what you've already covered yourself, what scares you most. Once it's said, you can hear it. Some of it is as bad as you thought. Some of it was the 3 a.m. version, and you'll notice the difference when you hear it in daylight.

It also helps to say the part about the people. The guilt, the sense that their families depend on a balance you can't promise. That part rarely gets said, because there's nobody to say it to who isn't affected by it.

## What the hour looks like

You can call from anywhere, or meet in person in Austin at noon on one of a few Wednesdays a month, somewhere public that we pick after you book. A first name is enough, and Stripe takes the payment, so I never see your card.

Before we start, you tell me if you want to be talked up or want to let it out. Some days you need a reminder that you built something people show up for. Some days you need to say every bitter thing about the customer who still hasn't paid. I won't offer advice unless you ask for it out loud, and silence is fine.

I've worked in payroll, so you won't have to explain what a run is or why the timing matters. I don't record anything, I don't take notes, and nothing you tell me gets repeated or used as an example.

## What it won't do

An hour of being listened to won't put money in the account. If you need help with the numbers, start with your accountant or a CPA who knows small businesses. If you need options for bridging the gap, a small business advisor or a lender who works with companies your size can walk you through them. I'm not a financial advisor and I won't tell you what to do with your cash.

If you're in crisis, call or text 988 in the US.

If you need to say it to someone before payday, a phone hour is $60, and you can book it under a first name. Book an hour.

## When you're getting divorced and your friends are picking sides

URL: https://jlisten2me.com/journal/friends-picking-sides/
Published: 2026-10-20
Author: John Parsons

The group chat went quiet around the time the paperwork started.
The weekend barbecue happened anyway, and you saw the photos afterward.
A couple you've known for years still texts your ex on birthdays and hasn't texted you at all.
On the weekends the kids are at the other house, the hours stretch out with nobody to fill them.

Divorce changes who you live with, and then, more slowly, it changes who calls. Some friends pull back because they don't know what to say and are afraid of saying the wrong thing. Some heard your ex's version first and settled on it before you'd said a word. And in a circle built around couples, you've become the odd number at the table.

## Why the people around you can't hold it

Mutual friends are the obvious ones to talk to, and the riskiest. Anything you say can reach your ex by the weekend, sometimes word for word, sometimes worse. Even the ones who mean well get asked, and most of them are bad at pretending they haven't heard anything.

The friends who stayed close tend to make every conversation about the divorce. You meet for a drink, and within five minutes it's the lawyer, the schedule, the house. You're grateful they ask. You'd also like one evening where you get to be a person instead of a case file.

Family has feelings about your ex too. Some relatives are angry on your behalf, and their anger becomes one more thing you have to manage. Others were fond of your ex and still are, and you can hear them working to stay neutral. Either way, you end up editing what you say before you say it.

Your lawyer is on your side, and your lawyer bills by the hour. Their job is the case. Spending a billable hour on the birthday dinner nobody invited you to makes no sense to either of you, so you hold that part back.

That leaves the loneliest part of the whole thing, the part about who's still in your life, with nowhere to go.

## Saying it to someone outside the circle

Losing friends in a divorce is a strange, slow kind of grief. It happens through silence: a missing invite, a slower reply, a conversation that stops when you walk in. Saying it out loud gives it edges. You can name the people one at a time, say what each of them meant to you, and hear how much of your ordinary week went with them.

It also matters to talk to someone who has heard nothing from your ex. There's no version of the story to correct and no impression to defend yourself against. You get to tell it from the beginning, in your own words, to someone with no side to pick and no reason to repeat it.

You can say the unflattering parts too: the hurt at being left out, the anger at a friend who should have known better, the relief about one or two who drifted. Those are hard to say to anyone who might be at the next party.

## What the hour looks like here

You can talk by phone from anywhere, or meet in person in Austin on a Wednesday at noon, at a public spot we agree on after you book. A first name is enough. Stripe takes the payment, so I never see your card.

At the start, you tell me whether you want to be talked up or want to let it out. On a weekend with the house empty, either one is a reasonable choice. I don't give advice unless you ask for it out loud. Silence is fine.

I don't take notes and nothing is recorded. I don't know your ex or anyone in your circle, and nothing you say is repeated or ever used as an example.

## Who's better for the rest

An hour of being listened to won't repair friendships, and it has nothing to do with how your divorce turns out. Your lawyer is the person for the case itself, and anything about custody, money, or what you should or shouldn't say publicly belongs with them. If you want steady support through the months ahead, a therapist or a divorce support group can offer it over time, with the same people week after week.

If you're in crisis, call or text 988 in the US.

If you'd like an hour with someone who hasn't heard either side, a phone hour is $60, booked under a first name. Pick a time.

## When you have to decide and can't tell anyone yet

URL: https://jlisten2me.com/journal/decision-you-cant-share/
Published: 2026-10-13
Author: John Parsons

You know the number before anyone else does.
Maybe it's runway: eleven months on the spreadsheet, closer to seven once you stop being generous with the forecast.
Maybe it's a list of names.
Maybe it's an offer for the company, sitting in your inbox while you decide whether to answer it.
Whatever it is, you're holding it alone, and you'll keep holding it until you know what you're going to do.

That stretch between knowing and deciding wears you down in a particular way. You walk into Monday's meeting with a level face. You answer "how's it going" with "busy." You get home, someone asks how your day was, and you pick the version that won't keep them up.

## Why the usual people can't take it

Every person you'd normally talk to has a reason they can't hear this one yet.

Your team would hear it as a forecast. Mention to your head of engineering that you're worried about spring payroll, and by Thursday two good people have quietly updated their résumés. That's a sensible reaction to what you told them, and it's exactly why you can't tell them until you've decided.

Your cofounder or partners have money and years in this too. Bring them a doubt and they'll bring their own position to it. You wanted to think out loud, and twenty minutes later you're negotiating.

Your board and investors are the people you'll eventually owe a plan. Show up with an open question and they'll hear a leader who's wobbling. Some of them will start making their own calls before you've made yours.

Your spouse or partner will listen. They always do. Then they'll carry it with you, at two in the morning, on top of everything they already carry. Most people in your seat stop bringing it home after the first few times they see that happen.

Friends in your industry know people who know your people. Austin is a small town once you're a few years into any field.

Advisors, coaches, and lawyers are useful, and you'll need some of them. They're also paid to move you toward an answer. Some days what you need is to hear what you think before anyone moves you anywhere.

## What saying it out loud does

Inside your head, a decision like this loops. The same three options come around, the same worst case, the same line you'd use in the all-hands. Looping feels like thinking, and it can go on for weeks.

Saying it to another person forces it into order. You have to start somewhere, and where you start tells you something. You hear which part you rushed past. You hear yourself argue for the option you thought you'd already ruled out. Sometimes you hear that you made the call a while ago and have been waiting for someone to let you say it.

The other person barely has to do anything. They have to stay quiet, keep up, and have no reaction that matters to you. That combination is hard to find in your own life, because everyone in your life is connected to the outcome.

## What the hour looks like

You book a time, by phone from anywhere or in person in Austin on a Wednesday at noon. You can book under a first name. Stripe handles the payment, so I never see your card.

When the call starts, you say whether you want to be talked up or want to let it out. If you'd like a question or two back, ask, and you'll get them. Then you talk. You can start in the middle. You can spend twenty minutes on the spreadsheet and ten on how you feel about the people on the list. Silence is fine.

I don't take notes and nothing is recorded. I'm not on your cap table, I don't work in your industry, and I don't know your investors. When the hour ends, the only person who leaves with any of it is you.

## What it won't do

An hour of being listened to won't make the decision for you, and it won't make it right. If you're working out severance, notice periods, or what you're allowed to tell employees, you need an employment lawyer. If it's the numbers themselves, you need your accountant or CFO. If the weight has turned into weeks of bad sleep, or into something you can't shake when the work is done, a licensed therapist is the right person, and I'll say so plainly if it comes up.

If you're in crisis, call or text 988 in the US.

If you're carrying one of these right now, a phone hour is $60 and you can book it under a first name. Pick a time.
